items.source: Ребята, на его месте должен был быть… я! — Напьёшься — будешь
items.reference: Guys, I should have been in his place! — Get drunk enough, and you will be!

general.text: A clash of registers. Gorbunkov is in full 'spy thriller' mode; he sees a body being carried and assumes the smugglers have struck again. His statement is a heavy, sacrificial declaration of a hero who thinks he dodged a bullet. The policeman, performing a routine 'drunk tank' pickup, is bored and amused. His response is a classic piece of 'cop humor'—mocking the dramatic tone by treating 'being carried away' as an inevitable destination reached through enough alcohol consumption.

items.candidate:
I should be in his place.
Get drunk and you will be!

issues.justification: The dramatic, sacrificial tone of Gorbunkov's declaration is flattened, and the cop's retort lacks the mocking 'enough' (drink enough and you will be) so the deadpan sarcasm is weaker, though the basic joke survives.

items.source: Я не трус… но я боюсь
items.reference: I'm no coward... but I'm overpowered by fear!

general.text: A relatable human paradox that separates moral character ('not a coward') from the physiological reality of fear ('but I am afraid'). It captures the 'little man' forced into a 'big situation' who maintains his dignity while admitting his vulnerability. The rhythmic 'Trus/Boyus' rhyme in Russian provides a 'bouncing' effect that makes the admission feel lighthearted and endearing rather than pathetic.
general.nb: ***Things to avoid:*** literal translation that does not create any comic effect.

items.candidate:
No, I’m not a coward,
but I’m afraid...

issues.justification: Literal rendering with no comic effect, which the analysis explicitly says to avoid. The bouncing trus/boyus rhyme and the playful paradox are lost, and the added 'No,' makes it flat.

items.source: У Вас… ус… отклеился
items.reference: Um... your... mustache... is peeling off.

general.text: The ultimate exposure of the villain's facade through Gorbunkov's polite, almost helpful honesty in a moment of high tension. Pointing out a trivial failure, like a loose fake mustache, completely undermines the criminal's 'professionalism' and highlights the absurdity of their attempts at intrigue.

items.candidate: Your... mustache came unstuck...

issues.justification: The hesitant, stammering politeness (Um... your... mustache...) is partly kept, but 'came unstuck' is slightly stiff and the broken-off 'ус... отклеился' rhythm is weaker.

items.source: Леди, синьора, фрау, мисс, к сожалению, ничего не выйдет… Руссо туристо! Облико морале! Ферштейн?
items.reference: Lady, signora, frau, miss... unfortunately, nothing's going to happen. Russo Turisto! Obliko Morale! Verstehen?

general.text: A comedic mix of 'International' jargon. Gena attempts to project high Soviet moral standards using a mashup of loanwords to project sophistication. It is a performance of 'Western' worldliness by a low-level crook desperately trying to maintain a 'pure' image abroad.

items.candidate:
You know, signora, frau, miss,
unfortunately nothing will come of it!
Russo tourist...
Obliko morale... verstehen?

issues.justification: 'Lady' is mistranslated/replaced by 'You know', which loses the string of international address forms. 'Russo tourist' also loses the pseudo-Italian 'turisto', weakening the mashup of fake foreign words that is the core of the joke.

items.source: Шеф, всё пропало, всё пропало! Гипс снимают, клиент уезжает…
items.reference: Boss, everything's lost, everything's lost! The cast is coming off, the client is leaving!

general.text: The moment Gena's suave smuggler persona shatters into pure hysteria. The comedy stems from the transition of abstract panic ('Everything is lost!') to the absurdly specific detail of the medical cast—the literal safe for the diamonds—being removed prematurely.

items.candidate:
Boss, it’s all lost! All lost!!!
They’re removing the cast, the client is leaving.

items.source: Как говорит наш любимый шеф: «Если человек идиот, то это надолго»!
items.reference: As our beloved boss says: 'If a man is an idiot, it's for a long time!'

general.text: A blunt insult delivered as profound wisdom from an authority figure. The phrase 'это надолго' (for a long time) implies that idiocy is a chronic, incurable medical condition rather than a temporary lapse, delivered with cold, diagnostic finality.

items.candidate:
As our beloved Boss says,
if a man’s an idiot—
it’s for the long haul.

items.source: Дитя́м — мороженое, его бабе — цветы. Смотры, нэ пэрэпутай!.. Кутузоу!
items.reference: Ice cream for the young'uns, flowers for his broad. Look now, don't mix 'em up! Kutuzov!

general.text: Lyolik uses his characteristic speech style (non-standard, uneducated-sounding) to micro-manage Gena, who he (correctly) thinks so absent-minded that he might give the flowers to the children and ice cream to the wife. Calling the bandaged Gena 'Kutuzov' adds a layer of sarcastic historical mockery, comparing the bungling smuggler to the one-eyed Napoleonic-era General.

items.candidate:
ice cream for the kids,
flowers for his woman.
Don’t mix it up!
Kutuzov!

issues.justification: Lyolik's non-standard, uneducated speech style (nэ пэрэпутай, 'broad', 'young'uns') is not conveyed; the register is neutral and 'Look now' is omitted. Kutuzov is kept but with no marker of the sarcasm.

items.source: Как говорит наш дорогой шеф, за чужой счёт пьют даже трезвенники… и язвенники!
items.reference: On someone else's dime, even teetotalers and convalescers drink!

general.text: Cynical underworld philosophy suggesting greed is the ultimate human motivator, overriding both moral and medical convictions. The original Russian uses identical suffixes and rhythmic weight (trezvenniki/yazvenniki) to create a balanced, proverbial 'law of nature' feel regarding the allure of free alcohol.
general.nb: ***Things to avoid:*** no rythm whatsover; at least some creative solution must be present.

items.candidate:
As our dear Boss says,
even teetotalers drink
on someone else’s dime—
and ulcer sufferers too.

issues.justification: The analysis requires rhythm and a creative solution for the parallel trezvenniki/yazvenniki suffixes. The candidate is a plain literal rendering that splits the pair, with 'ulcer sufferers too' tacked on as an afterthought, losing the proverbial balance.

items.source: Шампанское по утрам пьют или аристократы, или дегенераты
items.reference: In the morning, champagne is drunk only by aristocrats and degenerates.

general.text: A rhyming social law delivered with Lyolik's gravelly authority. The humor stems from a hardened thug offering a sophisticated observation on the duality of early-morning drinking, effectively labeling himself and his partner in the process.

items.candidate:
Champagne in the morning is drunk
either by aristocrats or degenerates!

issues.justification: The rhyme aristocrats/degenerates is not exploited, and the gravelly proverbial authority is neutral. The awkward passive 'is drunk' is kept, but the content is accurate.

items.source: Достаточно одной таблэтки
items.reference: Just one 'tab-LEHT' will do.

general.text: A sinister display of 'pharmacological' efficiency. Lyolik’s specific mispronunciation of 'tablet' (table-t-ka with a hard 'e') makes the phrase funny and memorable.

items.candidate: One pill is enough...

issues.justification: The mispronunciation of 'tablet' that the analysis names as what makes the line funny and memorable is entirely lost; 'One pill is enough' is neutral and flat.

items.source: Наши люди в булочную на такси не ездят
items.reference: Our people don't take taxis to the bakery!

general.text: A defining statement of Soviet moral boundaries and surveillance. The Upravdom monitors 'purity' by labeling a taxi ride for a mundane errand (buying bread) as a suspicious sign of bourgeois excess, emphasizing the collective mindset and forced modesty of the era.

items.candidate:
Our people
don’t take taxis to the bakery!

items.source: Семё-он Семёныч!
items.reference: Semyo-o-on Semyonych!

general.text: A melodic, elongated sigh of disappointment. This patronymic address functions as a gentle 'facepalm,' expressing the weary patience of a professional handler or teacher dealing with Gorbunkov's constant bumbling and literal-mindedness.

items.candidate: Semyon Semyonovich...

issues.justification: The elongated, melodic sigh ('Семё-он') that conveys weary patience is lost; the plain full name with ellipsis only partly conveys the 'facepalm' tone.

items.source: Чтоб ты жил… на одну… зарплату!
items.reference: May you live... on nothing but... your salary!

general.text: A 'curse' that subverts expectations. In the Soviet shadow economy, living solely on a state salary implied poverty and a lack of access to 'deficit' goods. Lyolik delivers this with the theatrical weight of a death sentence, cursing Gena with the horror of an honest life.

items.candidate:
May you live
on one
salary!

issues.justification: 'On one salary' loses the 'nothing but' sense of living exclusively on a salary, which weakens the curse's force, though the staccato delivery in line breaks preserves some theatrical weight.

items.source: Цигель-цигель, цигель, ай-лю-лю
items.reference: Zigel-zigel, zigel, ai-lyu-lyu!

general.text: Gibberish urgency. 'Zigel' acts as a sharp command for speed, while the soft 'ai-lyu-lyu' reflects the distraction of the lady's advances. It is a rhythmic catchphrase for frantic rushing in a confusing environment.

items.candidate:
Lunda khanamarun, tsigel, tsigel, tsigel, ai-lyulyu...
Lyuche paron, ai-lyulyu, ai-lyulyu...

issues.justification: The candidate introduces unrelated gibberish ('Lunda khanamarun... Lyuche paron') not in the source, which is a different phrase altogether; the core 'tsigel, tsigel, ai-lyu-lyu' is only partly present and the line is added to.

items.source: Поскользнулся. Упал. Закрытый перелом. Потерял сознание. Очнулся — гипс
items.reference: Slipped. Fell. Closed fracture. Passed out. Woke up in a cast.

general.text: A staccato, telegraphic alibi. The comedy lies in how Gorbunkov repeats this rehearsed script literally and frequently to everyone he meets, turning a traumatic event into a rhythmic, suspicious mantra of mechanical honesty.

items.candidate:
slipped, fell...
closed fracture...
Lost consciousness, came to—
cast!

items.source: Лёгким движением руки брюки превращаются… Брюки превращаются… Превращаются брюки… В элегантные шорты
items.reference: With a light flick of the wrist, the trousers transform... The trousers transform... Transform, the trousers do... into elegant shorts.

general.text: The contrast between the promise of 'light' elegance and the physical reality of a stuck zipper. The desperate repetition captures the universal fear of a public malfunction, ending in the forced confidence of calling the ruined result 'elegant'.

items.candidate:
With a simple flick of the wrist,
the trousers turn into...
the trousers turn into...
the trousers turn into...
elegant shorts!

issues.justification: The repetition is rendered as a triple repeat of the same phrase and loses the reordered variation ('Transform, the trousers do...'); 'simple' instead of 'light' also slightly weakens the 'light elegance' promise.

items.source: Не виноватая я! Он сам пришёл!
items.reference: Twasn't my fault! He came here on his own!

general.text: A parody of high-drama seductress tropes. The comedy is driven by her morphological slip—using the 'uneducated' full-adjective form 'vinovataya'—revealing that her sophisticated facade is just a mask. She reverts to a provincial register when panicked.

items.candidate: It’s not my fault! He came by himself!

issues.justification: The analysis says the joke is the uneducated, provincial slip in 'Не виноватая я'. The candidate uses standard, neutral English, so the character's mask slipping into a provincial register is lost.

items.source: Кто возьмёт билетов пачку, тот получит… — Водокачку!
items.reference: Buy a whole ticket pack, win... a tractor rack!

general.text: A rhythmic anti-climax. The Upravdom's attempt at an upbeat lottery slogan is met with the sarcastic retort of an 'industrial' prize. It mocks the forced state lotteries and the absurdity of receiving a useless industrial object as a 'reward'.

items.candidate:
Whoever buys a stack of tickets gets...
A water tower!

issues.justification: The rhyme (пачку/водокачку) and the rhythmic anti-climax are lost, and the retort is merged into the same speaker's line with no sarcastic interruption; 'water tower' is a mistranslation of 'водокачка' (pump station) with no creative rhyming solution.

items.source: А если не будут брать - отключим газ!
items.reference: And if they won't buy them—we'll shut off the gas!

general.text: Totalitarian escalation over a minor task. When people won't 'voluntarily' buy lottery tickets, her immediate solution is to cut off a vital utility. It perfectly summarizes her character as a petty tyrant wielding absolute local power over the collective.

items.candidate:
- And if they...? And...
- And if they won’t buy—then we’ll cut off the gas!

issues.justification: The added, fragmentary '- And if they...? And...' is awkward and does not match the source line, though the tyrannical threat of cutting the gas is kept.

items.source: Ну, будете у нас на Колыме!.. — Нет, уж лучше Вы к нам!
items.reference: Well, if you're ever in Kolyma... — No, better you visit us!

general.text: A joke based on Soviet geography. Kolyma was synonymous with labor camps; while the guest offers a sincere invitation from his home region, Gena hears it as a threat of imprisonment. His polite, reflexive rejection is a classic cultural response to perceived danger.

items.candidate:
Well, if you’re ever in Kolyma...
No, better you come to us!

items.source: В таком виде… я не могу. Мне нужно… сначала… принять вѫнну, выпить чашечку кофэ…
items.reference: In this state... I simply cannot. I must first... bathe... and have a cup of 'coff-ey'...

general.text: Gena's affected pronunciation ('kof-e') is a marker of someone desperately trying to sound sophisticated while in a state of disarray. His misplaced priorities—insisting on a bath and 'fancy' coffee mid-crisis—highlight his 'aristocratic' delusions.

items.candidate:
Looking like this...
I can’t.
I have to... first...
take a ba-ath,
have a cup of coffee...

issues.justification: The affected pronunciation of 'кофэ' is not rendered (plain 'coffee'); 'ba-ath' gives some of the affectation, and 'принять ванну' is covered, so the loss is partial.

items.source: — А у вас нет такого же, но с пелра… с перламутровыми пуговицами? — К сожалению, нет. — Нет? Будем искать…
items.reference: — You wouldn't have the same one, but with mother-of-pearl buttons? — Unfortunately, no. — No? Must keep looking then!

general.text: A 'deficit economy' stalling tactic. In the USSR, shoppers took whatever was in stock; asking for a specific aesthetic detail like 'pearl buttons' was a polite but ridiculous way to reject an item and linger in a shop without looking like a spy.

items.candidate:
And do you have the same thing, but
with mother-of-pearl buttons?
Unfortunately, no...
No, huh... we’ll keep looking...

issues.justification: 'No, huh...' adds a flippant tone not in the source, and the stalling-tactic politeness ('Будем искать' as a deliberate lingering) is slightly weakened; the Gorbunkov stumble (пелра...) is omitted.

items.source: Нет! На это я пойтить не могу!
items.reference: No! I ain't doing no such thing!

general.text: A stubborn refusal using an intentionally incorrect, 'folksy' form of the verb 'to go' (poytit). The linguistic error adds a layer of stubborn, rural-sounding emphasis to the refusal, making the moral stance seem both absolute and slightly comical.

items.candidate: No, I can’t go along with that!

issues.justification: The deliberately incorrect, folksy 'пойтить' is the core of the line; the candidate's standard, formal 'I can't go along with that' removes the rural-sounding emphasis and comic effect.
